Do not use em dashes.

text:
In the late summer of 1854, a terrible sickness fell on Soho, a crowded district of London. The disease was cholera, and it killed with frightening speed. A healthy person could feel well in the morning, be racked with vomiting and diarrhea by afternoon, and be dead within a day or two, their body drained of fluid and their skin turned a grey-blue. In just ten days, more than five hundred people living within a few streets of one another had died.

At that time, almost every educated person believed cholera spread through "miasma," meaning foul air rising from rotting waste, sewers and swamps. The smell of a place was thought to carry the sickness. Germs were not yet understood, and nobody knew that tiny living organisms could cause disease.

John Snow, a physician living nearby, was one of the few who doubted this. He had been born to a poor family in York, trained as a surgeon's apprentice, and become a respected doctor in London. He was known for pioneering the use of anesthesia, and he had even given chloroform to Queen Victoria during childbirth. Years earlier, during an earlier cholera epidemic, he had noticed something that did not fit the foul air idea. Cholera seemed to attack the gut first, not the lungs. If bad air were the cause, he reasoned, why would the illness begin in the stomach? He suspected that people were swallowing something, and that the poison was passing from one person to another through contaminated water.

When the Soho outbreak began, Snow had a chance to test his idea. He did not sit in a study and theorize. He walked the streets and knocked on doors. He wanted to know who had fallen ill, who had died, and where they lived. He obtained the official death records and began marking each death on a map of the neighborhood, one small bar at a time, stacked at each address.

A pattern appeared. The deaths clustered thickly around one spot, a public water pump on Broad Street. Households near that pump suffered most, and the further from it you looked, the fewer deaths there were. To a modern eye this looks obvious, but at the time the idea of a map revealing the cause of a disease was new.

Snow did not stop with the map, because he knew a pattern alone could be argued away. He wanted to explain the exceptions too, and the exceptions turned out to be the most convincing part of the case.

Near the pump stood a workhouse housing about five hundred poor residents. Remarkably few of them died. Snow discovered the workhouse had its own well and did not rely on the Broad Street pump. A nearby brewery had many workers, and none of them died of cholera. The men were given free beer as part of their pay, and they largely drank that instead of pump water. It was a strange detail, but it fit his theory.

Then there was a puzzling case far from Soho. A widow living in Hampstead, several miles away, died of cholera. Snow learned that she had once lived in Soho and had loved the taste of the Broad Street water so much that she had it carried to her home every day. Her niece, who visited and drank some of the same water, also died. Neither lived near the outbreak, yet both had drunk from the pump.

By early September, Snow felt confident enough to take his findings to the local board of guardians, the officials who governed the parish. On September 8, he persuaded them to remove the handle of the Broad Street pump, so that no one could draw water from it. The outbreak was already declining by then, probably because many residents had fled the area, and some later argued that removing the handle made little difference. But the act became famous, a symbol of acting on evidence even when the full explanation was not yet accepted.

The authorities did not embrace his conclusion. A later inquiry by the parish found no proof that the pump was to blame. Officials were reluctant to believe that water, rather than air, carried the disease, partly because the idea was unpleasant and partly because it threatened established views.

Help came from an unlikely source. A local clergyman, the Reverend Henry Whitehead, had been skeptical of Snow's theory. But he knew the neighborhood and its people well. Investigating on his own, he found the likely starting point of the outbreak. An infant living at 40 Broad Street had died of cholera just before the epidemic began, and the family had washed her soiled diapers in a bucket and emptied the water into a leaking cesspool only a few feet from the pump's well. Contaminated water had seeped into the supply. Whitehead came to accept Snow's view and worked with him afterward.

Snow died in 1858, not yet knowing that his reasoning would be proven right. Only later, when scientists identified the bacterium that causes cholera, did his theory become accepted fact. Today he is remembered as a founder of modern epidemiology, the study of how disease spreads through populations. His map, his door-to-door questions and his careful attention to the exceptions remain a model of how to find a hidden cause by looking closely at where and to whom things happen.
